hint_dispositions.reason: T1218's image_load analytic targets the DLL-load proxy variants of the technique (rundll32/regsvr32 loading an attacker DLL). This rule fires specifically on squirrel.exe/update.exe with --download/--update/--updateRollback= and an http URL — a download/ingress and child-process proxy primitive, not a DLL-load proxy. Squirrel proxies execution by fetching a NuGet package and spawning a child process (becoming its parent), never by loading a DLL into itself, so image_load events on this binary return normal updater module-load volume without precision for the abuse. hint_dispositions.hint: logsource 'image_load' (recommended by techniques: T1055) is not covered — pull in cue_image_load.* or author a custom question with `category: image_load`
hint_dispositions.reason: The generic T1055 image_load analytic targets reflective/unusual DLL loads inside a victim process during classic injection. CoercedPotato does not inject a DLL — it impersonates a named-pipe token and calls CreateProcessWithTokenW, which leaves no anomalous image_load on a remote process. An image_load query would return ordinary module loads of CoercedPotato.exe itself with no precision for this mechanism. The mechanism is covered via process_creation evidence in Q6 (coercion source + elevated spawn) instead.

hint_dispositions.hint: logsource 'process_access' (recommended by techniques: T1055) is not covered and no template family exists — author a custom question with `category: process_access`
hint_dispositions.reason: process_access (Sysmon EID 10) detects handle opens against a target process with injection-class access masks (PROCESS_VM_WRITE, etc.). CoercedPotato's token theft uses OpenThreadToken against the impersonating thread, not a cross-process VM-write handle, so a process_access GrantedAccess query keyed to injection masks would not surface this tool's behavior. The token-acquisition step is covered behaviorally in Q6 (which SYSTEM process connected and whether its token was impersonated) using available process_creation evidence. No process_access question authored.

The behavioral objective is captured by the follow_on child chain and the network_connection egress question. No registry_set question authored.

playbooks.name: MMC Spawning Windows Shell

The rule fires when the parent process ends in mmc.exe AND the child is one of those binaries.

What other child processes did this same mmc.exe instance spawn?
What exactly did the spawned process do? Decode its full command line.
Which of the DCOM-abused binaries spawned, and is it the genuine signed system binary or a renamed copy?
Was there a network logon to this host immediately before mmc.exe spawned the child?
What host initiated the RPC connection to this system, and is it an expected administrative source?
What modules loaded into the spawned process or its host shortly after it started?
If the spawned child was PowerShell, was the command encoded, and what does it decode to?
Does mmc.exe normally spawn command interpreters or system utilities on this host?
Has this user previously produced the rule's pattern, and does that history fit their role?
Has this parent process historically driven the rule's pattern on this host or across the environment, or is the parent new for this activity?
Has this user account moved to other hosts using lateral-movement tooling?
Did other detections fire on this host in the hours before this alert?
Is mmc.exe spawning these same shells on other hosts in the environment?

The rule fires when a command line either contains a Defender preference cmdlet (Add-MpPreference or Set-MpPreference) together with a Disable* flag and an enabling value, OR contains the base64-encoded form

questions.question: Does the command line either invoke a Defender preference cmdlet with a Disable flag, or contain the encoded form of those options?
Is this user and host expected to change Defender protection settings?
Which specific Defender protection features were disabled in this command?
Was the command encoded or obfuscated, and what does it decode to?
Did PowerShell script block logging capture the deobfuscated script content?
Were PowerShell security controls bypassed or weakened around this execution?
What process spawned this PowerShell instance, and is that parent chain expected?
Were the same Defender features disabled directly through the registry on this host around the alert?
Is Defender currently restored, or is real-time protection still disabled on this host?
What activity occurred on this host after Defender protection was disabled?
Were other defense tampering actions performed on this host?
When this host previously fired this Defender-disable pattern, what parents and users drove it, and does the current alert fit that pattern?
Have other hosts fired this Defender-disable pattern in the past week, and does the spread look like automation or one-off activity?
Has this user previously produced the rule's pattern, and does that history fit their role?
Has this parent process historically driven the rule's pattern on this host or across the environment, or is the parent new for this activity?
What else did this user do across the environment around the time of this alert?
Did this same parent-driven pattern fire on other hosts in the same window — i.e., is this a coordinated automation rollout, or is the activity isolated to this host?
Did other detections fire on this host in the hours before this alert?

questions.question: Does keytool.exe appear as the parent, and which command interpreter or system binary did it spawn?
Is this host expected to run a Java application that invokes keytool, and is this user expected to drive it?
What started keytool.exe, and was it driven by a web request to a Java application?
Is the Java application that hosts keytool up to date with security patches?
What was the full keytool command line, and does it carry injected provider or class-loading arguments?
What exactly did the spawned child binary do? Decode its full command line.
What started keytool, and is that grandparent chain consistent with normal Java keystore management?
What other child processes did this same keytool instance spawn?
Has keytool.exe ever spawned this child binary on this host before?
Has this user previously produced the rule's pattern, and does that history fit their role?
Has this parent process historically driven the rule's pattern on this host or across the environment, or is the parent new for this activity?
What else did this account do across the environment around the time of the alert?
Did this same parent-driven pattern fire on other hosts in the same window — i.e., is this a coordinated automation rollout, or is the activity isolated to this host?
Did this same detection fire on other hosts, indicating multiple exploited application instances?
What other process activity occurred on this host around the time of the alert?
Did other detections fire on this host in the hours before this alert?
Were other process-based persistence mechanisms installed on this host after the alert?

recommended-only; this is a server-side exploitation signal where the disposition turns on the exploitation chain and patch status, not on change-management approval. host_user_context and initial_access questions cover the legitimacy judgment.

recommended-only; process-based persistence sweep retained as the primary follow-on persistence check. File-drop persistence overlaps and would add a slot without proportionate value for a parent-child exploitation rule whose primary follow-on is command execution.

questions.question: Did wfc.exe run, either by Image ending in \wfc.exe or by reporting an OriginalFileName of wfc.exe?
Is this user and host expected to compile and run .NET workflows with the Windows SDK Workflow Command-line Compiler?
Where does the wfc.exe that ran live, and is that path the expected Windows SDK install location?
What did wfc.exe compile and run? Decode its full command line and identify the XOML or source file it was given.
What process spawned wfc.exe, and is that parent chain expected for a workflow compile?
Did wfc.exe spawn a script host or proxy-execution binary such as powershell.exe, cmd.exe, rundll32.exe, regsvr32.exe, wscript.exe, or mshta.exe?
Did files appear in user-writable or atypical paths around the time wfc.exe ran, consistent with a compiled payload being written to disk?
Did wfc.exe load any unsigned or user-writable DLLs?
Did wfc.exe or its child processes make outbound network connections shortly after the compile?
Has this user previously produced the rule's pattern, and does that history fit their role?
Has this parent process historically driven the rule's pattern on this host or across the environment, or is the parent new for this activity?
What else did this user do across the network around this time?
Did this same parent-driven pattern fire on other hosts in the same window — i.e., is this a coordinated automation rollout, or is the activity isolated to this host?
What other activity occurred on this host around the time of the alert?
Did other detections fire on this host in the hours before this alert?
When this host has previously fired the rule's wfc.exe pattern, what parents and users normally drive it, and does the current alert fit?
Have other hosts fired the rule's wfc.exe pattern in the past week, and does the cross-host distribution look like consistent automation or one-off activity?

playbooks.name: Xwizard.EXE Execution From Non-Default Location
playbooks.description: Detects xwizard.exe (the Extensible Wizards Host Process) executing from any directory other than System32, SysWOW64, or WinSxS. The rule fires when the process image ends in xwizard.exe OR carries the embedded OriginalFileName xwizard.exe, AND the image path is NOT under one of those three trusted

questions.question: Is the alerting process xwizard.exe running from a directory other than System32, SysWOW64, or WinSxS?
Is this user/host expected to run xwizard.exe from a non-system directory?
Does the binary's metadata and hash confirm it is the genuine Microsoft xwizard.exe, or a substituted file?
What did xwizard.exe do? Decode the full command line, looking for RunWizard, a CLSID GUID, or the /taero /u flag pair.
What DLLs did xwizard.exe load, and were any loaded from the non-default working directory rather than System32?
When and how did xwizards.dll (or a companion DLL) arrive in the directory alongside the relocated binary?
Was a CLSID InProcServer32 or LocalServer32 registry value written on this host pointing a COM class at a non-System32 path?
Was a mark-of-the-web or alternate data stream written to the companion DLL or binary, indicating download origin?
What process spawned this xwizard.exe instance, and is that parent chain expected?
What child processes did xwizard.exe spawn afterward?
When this host previously fired this xwizard.exe pattern, what parents and users normally drove it, and does the current alert fit?
Has this user previously produced the rule's pattern, and does that history fit their role?
Has this parent process historically driven the rule's pattern on this host or across the environment, or is the parent new for this activity?
What else did this user do across the network around this time?
Did this same parent-driven pattern fire on other hosts in the same window — i.e., is this a coordinated automation rollout, or is the activity isolated to this host?
Did other detections fire on this host in the hours before this alert?
How often has this host fired the xwizard.exe non-default-location pattern over the past 90 days, and what command-line structures are typical?
Have other hosts fired this xwizard.exe pattern in the past week, and does the cross-host distribution look like automation or one-off activity?
